utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, may I call upon the Prosecutor to try to be as brief as possible with all these witnesses, because we intend to finish with the evidence by next Thursday -- Thursday of next week, I mean -- both with the rebuttal and with the rejoinder witnesses. So that means that we have to be as brief and as short as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your point is well taken, Mr. President. We will be as brief as possible. I will also make sure I have one of the headphones around my neck, as Mr. Tucker and I will both be speaking English, and therefore the risk is going to go too quickly. Just prior to commencing, I would clarify an area where I believe there is a little confusion as to the order of witnesses. This has been raised by Defence colleagues today. We have, this morning, Mr. Tucker, as you know, an investigator, and I anticipate his evidence certainly in chief to be very brief. Indeed, in view of the ruling of yesterday, we will be saved about 25 minutes for the lack of a video that would no longer be played. So I anticipate that, from my point of view, I really think he might be concluded within the hour. The next witness we are calling is a witness who has been served under Rule 94 bis as an expert witness. His evidence will be somewhat longer, but I am hopeful that I may conclude within not much more than a couple of hours. Now, that leaves one civilian witness who will be examined by Mr. Terrier. Then that, in fact, is the end of our witnesses for this week, because, very unfortunately, it proved totally impossible to have Mr. McLeod in The Hague before Monday of next week. So in a sense, I think we might have plenty of time, but, obviously, not time to waste. Very well. I'll commence the examination then, Mr. President. Thank you, sir. Oh, my friend has a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I don't know if my colleague the Prosecutor, since he now announced that we are going to hear an expert witness after the current witness, I don't know if he's referring to the same person. If he is referring to the same person that I'm thinking of, I got only this morning -- and I wish to notify the Trial Chamber of this -- a 37-page document -- only this morning it was on my desk -- concerning that witness. I don't know whether the contents of this document differ in comparison to what we have already received. If it is identical, then I don't know why we received a new document. At any rate, I'd have to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I can explain that position. In fact, if anybody is at a disadvantage with that document, it is currently ourselves, because it is in the Serbo or Croatian language. What has happened is that the expert witness, when he came yesterday and was spoken to, produced a document saying that this was essentially an improvement upon the statement he had given to our investigation. So, in fact, he has prepared a kind of report reflecting what was in that statement. He says it has just been referenced and made a slightly more professional exercise, as an expert witness, than the original statement he gave. I'm not personally in a position to know the full contents because I cannot read the language, to my discredit, but I felt it appropriate that immediately we received that document -- and it is a document he would like to use for cross-reference, as his kind of notes in preparation for Court -- that I would serve it immediately and we would have to await our translation. But I thought it was appropriate, at least, to give it to the Defence. I shall be working from the file statement in the actual presentation of the evidence. If anything else should arise, then clearly I think we can deal with it as it happens. As I say, at the moment my friend has the advantage. He can read it; I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On the other hand, Counsel Pavkovic is right in saying that he needs time to read it. So that means that if we finish with the present witness this morning, we can't start with the next witness today. I wonder whether you have the witness number --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- number 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- who previously was number 1, available today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The person concerned is already here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But there has been no opportunity yet to speak to her, and it is appropriate, obviously, that my learned friend has some time with the witness prior to her giving evidence. So I'm just hopeful that this does not raise a problem. The document that was handed to us was not invited. It was an exercise in goodwill by the expert witness trying to do his job well. He gave it to us yesterday. I thought at least the fairest and proper thing to do would be to disclose immediately, even if I don't refer to it directly myself in examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm actually thankful for my colleague having done this immediately and having given this to us, but you do have to understand me. I indeed have to see whether the contents are identical to those of the document that we had received. Until then, until I've seen it, I cannot even agree to having this document being taken as some kind of a basis, a background material, whatever, for questioning that expert witness. So I need time to prepare myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if I get on with this witness, we may be able to create a little time where my friends will be able to adjust themselves to this development.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Let us start with this witness and we will see later on. We will duly take into account the concerns expressed by Counsel Pavkovic, who is right, I think. He needs time to read this document. Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. Mr. Blaxill, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you please give the Court your full name?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: My name is Howard Tucker, and I'm an investigator with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Tucker, you have already given evidence in this case, I believe on the 17th of October of last year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Have you undertaken certain investigative missions subsequent to that time and, particularly, a mission on the 10th of December of 1998?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where did you go at that time?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I returned to the village of Ahmici in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the objective of your mission?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The objective of the mission was to return to the village, accompanied by one of the witnesses who has been identified by the protective number of Witness R, and to conduct a reconstruction of her recollections of the events that took place in the village on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And whilst you were conducting that particular exercise, did you carry out any other tasks, such as taking any kind of measurements, or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was in possession of a pair of military Zeiss range-finding binoculars, and with the aid of this technical equipment, I took certain measurements from certain locations within the village that were identified to me by Witness R.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you receive any instruction in the use of those binoculars?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I received instruction from a member of the military who was trained in the use of the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And did you, upon your return, prepare any kind of documentary record of the measurements and the locations where you took those measurements?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. When I returned to my office, I prepared a schedule of measurements and distances in relation to certain locations within the village which are identified by the court map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at a document, if you would, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 384 from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I note at the very top it appears to be dated the 7th of December, 1998. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to undertaking the mission, I prepared a precis of the measurements I was going to take and then completed the document when I returned and had completed the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, I hope we perhaps do not need to make reference at this point to a map of the area, but if you feel the need to, please ask, and we'll supply one for that use. Can you advise, as regards entry number 1, what or whose was House 50?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: House 50, Your Honours, is the house in the occupation of Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And House 51?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Is the house in the occupation of the witness identified by the letter "S."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And House B?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Is the house of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the other item there, up to the -- number 5 is the vegetable store; what and where was that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's the structure that's been identified by several of the witnesses as being on the property of Witness Q and is situated some 50 metres, approximately, from the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, in a depression built into the side of a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And could you comment, please, on your annotations at number 6 within that form?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. At Item 6, we see that I've actually noted something in italics. This is directly related to the wishes of Witness R to proceed through some undergrowth. Under taking advice from the security forces who were accompanying us, they suggested that it would be unsafe to do so because of the threat of mines. Therefore we stayed on the perimeter of the forest, of the wood, where I took what measurements that I could at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And just to explain a little further, how in fact do these binoculars that you were using -- how do they operate?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The binoculars are constructed with modern laser technology, and by the pressing of two buttons, one on the right-hand and one on the left-hand side of the casing of the binoculars, you can get accurate measurements of, firstly, the distance in metres; and secondly, the actual bearing from your location to the object that you've made a fix upon. And the accuracy of the range-finder binoculars is considered to be within 2 metres over a distance of 1.800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And physically, how do you actually sort of aim them? Is there some indicator that you have picked your target point?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you operate them in exactly the same way as you would a conventional pair of binoculars, and when you have fixed on the position of the object you wish to take a measurement and bearing of, when you actually depress one of the buttons -- it doesn't matter which one you operate first -- it actually puts into operation the laser light, and that actually pinpoints the fixed object you're looking at and then records either the bearing or the distance, depending on which button you depress first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Tucker. Did you return on any subsequent mission to that area in August of this year?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I returned on the 25th of August of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what were the objectives of that particular mission?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: On this occasion I returned with four witnesses, including Witness R. The object of the exercise was the same as in December of last year, and that was to undertake a witness reconstruction with all four, and with the same objectives as that of December, to be able to take some fixed positions, to take certain measurements, and to retrace the steps that the witnesses recounted that they took on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the method that you used to take the measurements on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I used a pair of Leica range-finding binoculars, which are the same specifications as the Zeiss I used in December of last year. I used specific poles to place at the points of recognition of each witness. I actually took each witness in turn, and as they identified certain locations, I marked that position with one of these metal poles, continued through the witness reconstruction until the conclusion of that witness. I then returned the witness to a secure vehicle, and that witness was then removed from the scene. I then proceeded with the second witness, and so forth, until the final -- fourth and final witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you subsequently prepare any form of documentary record of the measurements that you took on that mission?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I prepared a similar report to that of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in respect of how many of the witness reconstructions did you record the actual measurements?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I recorded two, and that was in respect of Witness R and Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like, again, to show a document to the witness, with the appropriate copies for Their Honours and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 385.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, do you recognise that particular document?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's the document I prepared upon the completion of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think you just mentioned, an answer ago, it was in respect of Witness R and Witness Q. That would appear to differ from the document. Can you explain that, sir? It appears -- at the top I see "Witness Q," and below that "Witness II."

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, it is. It's Witness Q, Witness II, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Tucker, now, you say that -- is that an accurate reflection of the measurements that you took on the day, the 25th of August, 1999?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And could you just tell us: Marker 1 is referred to at the very first entry under "Witness Q." Would you just explain precisely what that location was?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Marker 1 was actually placed by the Witness Q at the location that he identified to me where Witness R had been shot on the 16th of April, 1993, and at that location where he turned around and saw the accused Vlatko Kupreskic, with HVO soldiers, shooting at his direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And so from that point, Mr. Tucker, you took a measurement towards a particular house, and I refer you now to the sixth entry under "Witness Q." Would you just confirm that measurement that you took?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The overall measurement was 53 metres, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was the house that you refer to, quote, the Kupreskic house, was that in your line of vision at that time?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: It was from the second location of the measurement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: During the course of this exercise, Mr. Tucker, was any other location or object of interest pointed out to you by Witness Q?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Prior to commencing the reconstruction, Witness Q indicated to me that there may be items, personal items in the wooded area that he would able to identify to me during the course of the reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what action did you take after that place had been identified to you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: When Witness Q identified the location to me, I removed him from the area, returned to the scene, and proceeded to exhume the artefacts from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What precautions did you take in respect of the preservation of those artefacts?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: As each item was taken from the ground, I had the items contemporaneously recorded by a colleague of mine, Brid O'Toole, who was an investigator with the ICTY at the Sarajevo field office. Each item was placed individually into a bag. Once all the items had been taken from the ground, I returned the items to the Sarajevo field office, where they were laid out in a security room to dry, and they were subsequently removed by a forensic scenes-of-crime examiner, taken to the mortuary facilities at a location called Visoko, where the articles were photographed, washed, rephotographed, and catalogued, and returned to the Sarajevo field office for safekeeping and to preserve the continuity and the chain of custody of the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: After you had placed those into safe custody, did you have any further dealings with those artefacts?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. On the 8th of September I returned to the region. I took possession of the artefacts and took them to another location where I met two of the witnesses, Witness Q and Witness R, where I showed each of the witnesses in turn the items. Certain of the items were subsequently identified by each witness in turn. The items identified by the witnesses I recorded, and then prepared a separate report in relation to those articles and caused those identified artefacts to be photographed and prepared them in folders for the Court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have a further document to present, if you'd be so kind, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 386.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, do you recognise those documents?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. They're reports I prepared in respect of Witness R and Witness Q in respect of their identification of the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as we propose tendering all these documents, I'm clearly not going through item by item in a list that everybody can read for themselves -- it will save time -- but I will do so if you wish. Of the various items that you showed to Witness by the name "R", or the pseudonym "R," how many items were identified?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in respect to Witness R, she identified 21 out of a possible 47 artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Witness Q?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Witness Q, Your Honours, identified 25 out of 47 items.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And just generally speaking, what did they identify them as? In other words, as whose property?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Generally the -- their family possessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did they say anything else about those family possessions, as to the circumstances they parted company with them?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you cause any photographic record to be made in relation to the artefacts recovered?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All the artefacts were photographed, as you're aware, as they were being taken from the ground. They were then photographed when they'd been taken back to the Sarajevo field office to dry, and they were again photographed by Mr. Govender, who was the forensic scenes-of-crime examiner, who photographed each item prior-washing and post-washing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And for the purposes of today's hearing, have you prepared any form of album or collection of photographs to assist the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I prepared an album of photographs purely based on the identification by the witnesses, and the majority of the photographs contained in that album are the articles as they are after washing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, possess, if Their Honours or anyone wish to see them, do you possess any photographs of pre-washed condition artefacts, if called upon?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And as to the artefacts, where are they presently?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: They're currently in my possession -- or, at least, when I say "in my possession," they're locked in a secure office in my working area within this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Tucker, I would like you to have a look at this photographic album.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph album will be Prosecution Exhibit 387.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recognise, Mr. Tucker, the photographic album and the index thereto?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is that the photographic album that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: It is, sirs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regards to those artefacts, whereabouts in the ground did you find them in relation, let us say, to the point you've mentioned already of marker 1, which is the place where some -- allegedly people were shot, and perhaps also directly in relation to the house of Mr. Kupreskic, which is another focal point of the area.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The articles were actually located at a position approximately 7 metres from the spot that Witness Q identified to me as where he dragged his daughter, the Witness R.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And where is that in relation to what we've heard referred to as the hill or the ridge opposite of the house of Mr. Kupreskic, Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: It's actually on the top of the ridge, slightly out of -- it's out of sight of the Vlatko Kupreskic house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And are you able to or were you able to ascertain, in your investigation, who was carrying those artefacts when those artefacts found their way onto that hillside?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, sir. Your Honours, it appears that there were several family members involved in carrying these items, and it's uncertain who was carrying what at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move to a different subject, and that relates to dealings with a witness, a witness who will be a protected witness, and I think it would be appropriate to request, Your Honours, to go into private session for that purpose. We are going to have to discuss a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If all is well, I'll repeat the question. Yes, Mr. Tucker, the side of the hill facing the house of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic, do you recall or have your investigations revealed essentially how steep that was, and particularly in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the area where the Witness R was shot at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I understand that to be the area referred to.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The actual height of the inclination I'm not aware of. It's certainly not a gentle slope or gentle climb, but I wouldn't describe it as being as severe as the opposite side of the ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the opposite side of the ridge, how does that slope from the ridge?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The incline is quite considerably more than that on the opposite side. That is the side that faces the Vlatko Kupreskic house. And I must say the first time that I actually went there was with Witness II, and the climb was quite a severe one, especially the last 20 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: There's just one other point. It goes back to the beginning of your evidence. You identified houses by the name of -- numbered 50 and 51. There is something in the transcript -- I'm sorry. If I can interrupt with this. There is something in the transcript that appears a little unclear. It says: "From the opposite side of that ridge how does that slope ...", and it says, "The incline is quite considerably more on the opposite side. That is the side that faces Vlatko Kupreskic house." Which is the steeper one? The side facing the Kupreskic house or the other side?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The other side of the hill. The other side of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The other side is the steeper. Are you aware of any change of the terrain between the ridge and the house of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic that occurred since 1993?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I've had several references made by the witnesses, Your Honour, concerning the change of the landscape in the area between the ridge I've just described and the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, from an area that stretches from the point identified by the witnesses that they entered, the area known as the forest, stretching back as far as the vegetable store and even down almost to the house identified as house 50. I've had it described to me as having several hillocks that were in existence pre-1993, which have since been completely removed, and the landscape, as such, been backfilled in what has been described to me as the valleys, which is the short, if you like, the ravines in between these hillocks, and I think the evidence of this earthwork is quite evident on the video and film footage, and most certainly when you attend to the village of Ahmici. The change of the land is quite evident, quite visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just finally, Mr. Tucker, going back to where we started, you mentioned houses 50 and 51, and gave us some pseudonyms relevant thereto. Are you sure you're correct as to those pseudonyms, as to which was which occupant?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I may well have got them reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Okay, sir, thank you. Now, is it correct that in the course of your investigation in both August of 1998 and -- sorry, December of 1998 and August of 1999, did you, in fact, cause videotapes to be prepared and they were prepared?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And, in fact, as a matter of information, was the point of the -- where the property was found in the earth, was that point, in fact, included in one of those videos and identified in a video?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Identified in the video by the Witness Q. That was conducted on the 25th of August this year, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. That concludes my questioning. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic, who is going to cross-examine this witness? Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague Par will cross-examine the witness, and he will be the only one to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker. Before I ask you some questions related to these matters, I should like to resolve the problem of the lay of the land around Vlatko Kupreskic's house and the slopes and how steep they are on both sides; and to do away with this, I will give you the finding of a surveyor who testified here as an expert witness and gave us his opinion. In his report, he made a cross-section of that hillock and also attached a map. So would you please be so kind and have a look at this, and simply confirm or, again, deny that this map -- this cross-section of the ground tallies with your observations there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Usher, could you please place it on the ELMO? This was admitted into evidence. I don't have the number now, but when that expert witness Blaz Kesic, land surveyor -- it was tendered on that occasion and it is part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you find your ways around this? You can see Vlatko Kupreskic's house to the left and then the lines are showing the field of vision, and we have the height. Heights are indicated on one of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would that agree with your observations made on the ground? Is the sketch a true picture of those heights, those slopes, inclinations?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's -- it's certainly in keeping with what I've testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But before I ask my next question, I should like to mention that it was only this morning that the Defence received these photo documents and the identification by Witness F. Formerly we had the identification of various objects made by Witness Q, and we knew about that, but it was only this morning that we received the identification of these objects, and I'm afraid that this places us on a slightly inequitable footing. This is merely a remark; I do not wish to do anything about it, but I merely wanted to say that the Defence really tried very hard to disclose to the Prosecution all the material that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: However, Mr. Tucker, with regard to these measurements, I should like to seek the confirmation of some data; that is, measurements from the position where Witness Q, according to him, turned and looked in the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's house and saw soldiers and Vlatko Kupreskic. That is what he said. Did I understand you properly when you said that you measured the distance was 53 metres?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. Then let us move on to these personal effects, to these objects. Could you perhaps be more precise: Who was the first one to mention these objects? You said Witness Q, but could you tell us, what did he tell you, how did he find out about these things, how did he describe it to you, what language did he use, what words did he use?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was in the company of an interpreter at all times with the witness, and the witness explained to me that he believed that there were family artefacts -- or I shouldn't say "artefacts"; articles of clothing in the woods that we were about to enter, and that he knew approximately the location of where these articles should be, and that he should be able to point them out to us if we entered the wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That is what I really would like to know. Did he say that because he knew that those things were left behind in '93, or did he see them in '99 and then realise they belonged to such-and-such persons?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: It's my understanding that he discovered them in 1999, and he made his first identification to me on the video footage. As soon as he identified the items, I removed him from the scene and then began to excavate the items from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, I could see that on the tape. And did he dwell at length on how he found those articles? Why was he walking around those woods? Was he looking for them? Did he really give you a full account of how he came to find them?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And other witnesses, Witnesses R and S, did he ever mention those things, those personal effects, or indicate that they knew about them?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, they gave me no indication that they knew where they were, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you went to that place to look for those things with Witness Q, and as you were passing through the wood, did you see other discarded things, objects, around that place in the wood; that is, some other articles apart from those which Witness Q showed to you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Had I seen any other artefacts, then I would have recovered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: For instance, I saw -- and you may have; just to remind you -- there was an old water boiler not far from there, and then a car wreck, I think, was also somewhere around. Would you remember artefacts like that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I certainly remember the old water boiler, Your Honours, because it caused a bit of concern for the security forces at the time. I can't remember the vehicle wreck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. I mentioned this because we heard that it was a dump yard. When showing you the place where all these artefacts were, did Witness Q affirm that they had been lying there as of the 16th of April, '93, to the day when you went to look for them?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I don't recall his exact words, but the implication that I recall is certainly that they -- that they have laid there for the whole of the period since April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You mean you made that inference from what he told you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's my recollection, sir, from the conversation that we had in the woods at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I should particularly like to know if Witness Q also mentioned that those artefacts could have been moved about, because after all, six years have elapsed. Did he ever mention the possibility of their having been moved around, transferred from one spot to another, or were they lying discarded there for more than six years?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: There was certainly no dialogue by Witness Q about the property. As soon as the first items were identified on the surface to me, I removed him from the scene and continued to excavate the items. I probably should say, from my own observation, that I think it's unlikely that those objects had been moved, because there were so many in one spot that had they been moved or dumped or transferred, it's unlikely to have found so many family artefacts in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but let me ask you this: In the vicinity of the site -- that is, within a 10-metre radius or so -- did you notice any changes in the area? I mean, the woods, did you see some tree stumps? Did you see that the wood was felled and that what is growing there now is not the same wood that existed there in '93?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical to assume that they felled the trees, that the logs were taken away from that site? I am saying that as those logs were pulled out and as the trees were felled, all these artefacts, all these things may have been moved. So it is quite possible that when the trees were felled and pulled out, that those things could have been moved.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: There are many possibilities, sir. I don't think I am able to answer that particular question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Quite, quite. I quite get your point, and I am not asking you to say yes or no; I am simply trying to define all the possibilities, to say that it was possible to move them. I should also like to know if Witness Q mentioned on that occasion that some other groups of refugees used that same path, or did he say that those things there could only be the personal effects of members of his family?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Are you referring, sir, to the refugees who left the area with that particular family on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The 16th of April, I mean on the 16th of April; that same day, but not the same group. We heard testimonies here there was (redacted) group which also went through there, and they also cut some branches to make a stretcher for his wife and so on and so forth. So other groups also used that path on the 16th of April. Did perhaps Witness Q indicate that some of these things might belong to some other groups, or to people in some other groups?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. At all times the evidence related by all the witnesses was specifically about their own experiences on that day and relating purely to -- I'll refer to their group, which includes the refugees that they mentioned in their testimony, and the route that they actually took on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's all right. Very well. Mr. Tucker, please, if you look at the place where these things were found, did you notice any traces of fire, some burned wood, or something like that? Were there any signs of a fire there?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I didn't notice any signs of any fire in the wooded area at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at our photo documents now, number 5. That is part of a bag, a handbag, that was burned. You probably remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Right. A burned handbag. And then, under number 8, there is also a burned woollen sock. So that is now being contested. We see these two objects here in the pictures, that they were partly burned. Mr. Tucker, a few minutes ago you said in your statement that all these objects were practically in a single spot, all the objects that were retrieved; that is Location B, if I'm not mistaken. So was there anything on the ground that could explain how come some things were burned -- we know that wool and handbags would burn with great difficulty -- and other things were not touched by fire? Is there any explanation for that on the ground, that some of these objects were partly burned and others were not?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not convinced that any of the items were burned at all. In particular, the bag, 5, is a plastic bag; and plastic, as you probably are aware of yourself, sir, has different sort of methods of disintegrating in the ground, and to me it appears to be an old plastic bag that is gradually disintegrating. As regards item 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Tucker. I am not asserting that it's burned; that's what your document says, under number 8. I've got the report here saying, under number 8 -- or 5; that's the document that I received from the Prosecutor. Number 5, on the 25th of August, 1999, Location B, a bag, part of a bag that is burned. Again, the 25th of September, 1998, a partly burned woollen sock. That's the only thing I have, and it is on that basis that I made this assertion. Can you say that it's something different? Can you today say it's something different, that it wasn't burned, that it was a different kind of damage that was done to these objects?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: No, of course not, sir. I can't say that. What I'm saying is that it's an observation, and an observation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If we look at this sock under number 8, we will see -- perhaps we can see better in this photograph that this is a substance that was burning. Therefore my question is: How come -- of course I'm not asking you to give answers to questions that you cannot answer, but on the ground, is there any reason that would explain this, why this was burned, partly, and whether other things that would burn more easily were not burned at all? Is there anything on the ground to suggest how come this happened?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: There is nothing on the ground at all to explain it, but there could be explanations. I think in the testimony of several of the witnesses they referred to being shot up with exploding bullets and the like. It could have been caused by a fragment of shrapnel or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's right. I allow that possibility. However, then I would like to ask the following: Did Witness Q mention what happened to his other belongings that remained in his old house that was burned? Is it possible that some of these objects are from that burned house? Of course, I'm not asking you to answer that question, but I'm just asking you whether Witness Q mentioned that part of his belongings burned down in his old house. Did Witness Q mention that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Witness Q -- he had no reason to mention that at the time of finding the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perhaps he could have, in view of these things that were burned, but all right, he didn't. Let's move on further.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you -- I'm sorry, sir -- I'll make a point there. Witness Q wasn't aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Witness Q wasn't aware of these items being taken from the ground until he was shown them to identify them on the 8th of September this year, so he wouldn't have known of the appearance in the soil of them being burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tucker, we can see that there are quite a few woollen artefacts here; among other things, this red sweater, number 3. We can see it here, and it's very well-preserved. Furthermore, under number 31, we also have a blue garment that is impossible to identify. My question would be the following: On that location where these artefacts were, over there on the ground, were there any signs showing why objects made of the same substance, under the same conditions, would be damaged in such totally different ways during the same period of time, when nothing had happened to them, when they were not removed? Is there any clue on the ground why something would totally disintegrate, whereas a different object, made of the same material, would remain practically intact, if they were all there during those six years? Is there any clue?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I have two answers for that question, sir. The first one is that we don't know that all the material is made of the same and hasn't disintegrated in the same way. Secondly, I'm not a scientist and I'm not able to give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: One of the questions I wanted to put is whether you wanted some expertise to be carried out by chemistry experts or someone to see how old these objects were, in order to determine how old these objects were and under which conditions they deteriorated, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I personally feel that the identification of the items by the family and the location and the condition of the objects when they were retrieved from the ground is sufficient. That's what I believed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I apologise if you think that I'm too insistent with my questions, but I am a lawyer and I have to go through all of this. So please bear with me. Could you please have a look at photograph number 4? It is called an unidentified electric wire. That's what it's called in this list. There is no doubt that this wire was part of an electrical appliance, a hair-dryer or something to that effect; that is to say, nobody would carry around only an electric wire. So, now, on the ground there is only this electric wire. Where could this hair-dryer have disappeared? A hair-dryer could not have disintegrated, rotten away. Is there any clue as to what had happened? Can you see anything there?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Nothing at all, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let us conclude with this section, and now let us move on to the identification of items; that is to say, the 8th of September, 1999. Now, Witnesses R and Q are identifying those artefacts that you referred to today. Please, were R and Q together at the time when the identification was carried out or did they each do this on their own, separately?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Both witnesses were together at the start of the identification; that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We saw the things concerned and we saw what they had to say about this. Please, among all these things, was there a single item that was undeniably the Pezer family's? Was there anything that had to belong to the Pezer family and no other family, irrespective of their statements and everything? Could you please answer that and then we'll move on?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. In respect of Witness R, there were two items in particular -- beg your pardon, three items in particular that were undeniably identified, in my opinion. The first one was the red sweater that you've shown before the -- Your Honours this morning. The second item was item 9. It's photograph 9 in the album. Exhibit number 9. Each of these items are individually wrapped in clear plastic bags, and this particular T-shirt was folded in on itself so you couldn't see the logo on the front. Before it was removed from the bag, she made a comment that she thought it was a T-shirt with a round neck, a white T-shirt with a picture on it. It was black with numbers and letters, but I can't remember what. And of course, I opened up the package and took the shirt out, and then she made the identification. And then the second item in particular, or third item, I should say, was number 24, exhibit number 24. It was a similar situation. The photograph that you see, the second photograph, they're both of the same, pre and after watch. It shows clearly a pattern on the design, and she said, "I think it's a piece of my mother's clothes that I cut to make a headscarf." Of course, she was unaware that that was a headscarf before. She only saw it in its uncut condition. I say it was only three, but there was another item as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you. Thank you. Very well. My question was whether there was a single item that could not have belonged to anyone else, and your answer was that with a degree of liability, they recognised some of their own items. However, let us dwell on item 24. We're talking about a black headscarf that is part of her mother's clothing. However, I wanted to mention that particular item, and to say that that could not have belonged to her mother at all if it's a black headscarf, simply because women in Bosnia who wear black headscarves are only Serbo-Croat women. Muslim women never wear black headscarves. I've lived there all my life. I know that myself. Never, ever have I seen anything like it. So that is precisely the item I wished to contest, but that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon to me for rising, but with all due respect, Mr. Par is intending to give evidence to contradict the witness. Cross-examination is something different, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I am concluding my questioning with this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I thank you, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that particular point that the gentlemen made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: In actual fact, I didn't say that this -- I said it was a headscarf. It was my assumption because of the way it was found on the ground. What the witness told me is that it was a piece of her mother's clothing that she had cut to tie her own hair back; it wasn't a headscarf that belonged to her deceased mother, and that's what I said in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I was guided by what the paper here said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Par. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand, there's no other cross-examination, Mr. President. I have a couple of questions only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, when you commenced the reconstruction exercise with Witness Q, what was your main purpose?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The main purpose of the mission was to do a witness reconstruction, as I described earlier, to take measurements at points specified by these witnesses when they remembered them during the course of their exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And on the day when you prepared to do this exercise with Witness Q, were you then aware of any issue relating to property that might be in the ground?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That was the first time that I was aware of there being any suggestion of any property possibly belonging to any of the victims of this particular day in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And -- so following on, you commenced this exercise, and you were going through the woodlands. What, if any, other kinds of property did you see as you went through the wooded land and the undergrowth? Did you see any other household refuse or anything else of that nature?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Nothing at all that would indicate it as being a refuse tip of any description.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, that was my next question. Nothing indicating a public tip or a regularly used tip of that nature?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Thank you. You stated that Witness Q and Witness R were both present at the commencement of the identification of the articles of clothing and other artefacts?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, did they remain together throughout that exercise or was some or any portion of the identification carried out with them separately?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: The majority of the identification was carried out separately, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you recovered the goods in Bosnia and they were tendered to Sarajevo field office, was any record made to record them into the custody of your colleagues in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. A chain-of-custody record was prepared by my colleague Brid O'Toole in connection with the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you aware of how many, if any, items logged into the custody record were referred to as having in any way been burned or fire-damaged or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I'm not, no, sir. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you, in fact, recognise the custody record if it was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: I would, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In that event, Your Honours, I don't have all additional copies, at the present time, of this document. I would like to present it to the witness and show it to Your Honours and to the Defence. I will, obviously, have -- yes. Through the coffee break we can make sure you have all the adequate copies. Sorry, it's two sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that schedule and document, sir?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes. That's a photocopy of the original. It bears the signature of Brid O'Toole and Ronny Govender, the forensic science examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From the nature of the items that are listed, can you say whether or not that relates to the property recovered by you in the location in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm happy that they refer to the articles that I mentioned in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And just for a moment, Mr. Tucker, would you place that on the ELMO, and we could just look at the list of artefacts. Mr. Tucker, can you say -- with a quick glance through that list, can you identify or indicate how many you see there as marked in any way fire-damaged or burned?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: Item 5, portion of carrier bag, burned; item 8, one woollen sock, portion burned. And that, I believe, is it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tucker. Just one final thing to confirm. All the artefacts in question are presently in the custody of yourself within this building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I would wish now to do is, firstly, I will obviously indicate to you that if you wanted to see any or all of those artefacts, I would happily arrange for them to be produced in court for your convenience. For security reasons, and unless necessary, we obviously try not to disturb physical evidence any more than is necessary. The second thing, Your Honours, is that I would like to tender, please, the documentary evidence I have submitted. Thus far, I think, the numbers would be P384 through to P387, but with this latest addition, I think it would take us to P388. If you would accept those in evidence, subject to my friend's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection, Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, my objection is that the identification of items recovered from Ahmici on the 25th of August, 1999, that record be admitted into evidence. I object to that. I believe that these are registered comments of Witnesses Q and R, and the Defence was not in a position to cross-examine the witnesses on these statements of theirs; that is to say, to put further questions to them so that they could give more detailed explanations as to how they recognised the objects as belonging to themselves. If this record were to be admitted into evidence, then we would be taking these witness statements for granted, without giving the Defence the possibility to re-examine these witness. So this was carried out in Zenica, and Witness Q spoke about this and -- I have no further objections as far as other evidence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, clearly in that sense, the annotation of the comments of the witnesses in identifying the property are a hearsay record by an investigator. That is quite clear. We found that not to be an objectionable course in view of the stance taken by your Chamber and others with regard to hearsay evidence. You will value its weight and give it due weight, but at least make it admissible. So on that basis, Your Honours, we have put forward simply the fact that the investigator has placed the items forward before the people, elicited and recorded comments, and he has delivered that now essentially as a hearsay record. I suppose if there is an objection to the documentary record by the investigator coming before you, then with your leave I could suggest that that is an issue now in which I should re-examine and simply have him deliver oral evidence as to what his investigation in that respect revealed. I was hoping, however, we would save time simply by the comments being recorded and they can be read by Your Honours rather than taking up hours in the courtroom. But I'm happy to examine on that to make it quite clear, accepting, of course, that is hearsay evidence. I quite accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit this document P386 as hearsay evidence, and, of course, it is for us to decide what probative value it will be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then I think that does conclude business with this witness. I'd apply for his release, if you will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tucker, for giving evidence in court. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, at this stage we normally take a break, but before that I would like to ask Counsel Pavkovic whether he could probably, say, in one hour, go through that document so that we could resume our hearing in, say, one hour? Do you think one hour would be sufficient for you to go through that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not too sure, Mr. President, that that is sufficient time for me, only to read through it. Of course, I would have to compare it to the previous documents. But my other colleagues are also telling me that they would like to have information about the contents of this document, if they would possibly want to examine it themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You know, our problem is that we can't sit this afternoon because Judge May is sitting in a different case. I wonder whether we could then ask the Prosecutor to call the -- maybe in one or two hours, the other witness, number 1, the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think that gives us a serious difficulty, Your Honours. The other alternative is that, at this point, if we obviously would take the break now, and if we then carried on and listened to the evidence in chief of the expert witness, that might well take us through most, if not all, of the rest of the morning. Clearly, my friends could then re-evaluate their position with regard to cross-examination if they feel that this has caused them any difficulty. Equally, you might perhaps build in just a little extra time for the morning break and they could have a look through. The witness advises me that this document very much tracks the statement that has been already submitted. It is just, he feels, a more professional and polished version. As I say, I don't read the language, so I can't give you any formal undertaking to that end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think it's a very sensible suggestion. Counsel Pavkovic, we could, this morning, confine ourselves to examination-in-chief. So tomorrow we would -- whether or not we finish by 1.15, tomorrow we could start with the cross-examination. So you would have the whole afternoon to go through the document. All of you, I mean, all Defence counsel. Does sound acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm speaking in my own name -- well, I think my colleagues share my view. This seems to be a good proposal. However, Mr. President, nevertheless, I would like to point out some very important matters related to the statement of this witness. Of course, I won't do it now; I'll do it after the break. But there are a few matters that I wish to highlight because I wish to seek your assistance with regard to these matters. I know that our time is running out now, but perhaps when we resume it would be a good idea for me to bring up those questions then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we'll take now a 30-minute break. Then when we resume, you will make your comments or objections, and then we will start with the examination-in-chief of our next witness. All right. So we'll break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The latest Prosecution Exhibit, the exhibit that is in fact the document bearing the different names of the pieces of clothing found by the investigator in Sarajevo, is Exhibit Number 388.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may raise just one thing briefly: When you ruled in respect of videos that were offered both by the Prosecution and the Defence and that they should not be played, you did make specific reference to a portion of a video that had been put forward by the Prosecution relating only to the area where the property was found and any work undertaken there. I hadn't mentioned it previously. It is my mistake. I would like to rectify that, with your leave, and ask if we may formally tender that video in respect of that portion only, as it has been served on the Defence and on yourselves. I obviously didn't play it in court, Your Honours; I felt it might be just taking unnecessary time. If you feel there's a problem, I would be happy to recall Mr. Tucker appropriately, and we would play that portion to the Court. If the situation is acceptable without that, then, with my apology for not dealing with it sooner, I would ask to tender that one extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par? Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If it is only a portion of the tape recording how the investigator collected those things, then we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: For that question, I ask for nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Only that portion, only where Mr. Tucker collected the items. So it is admitted into evidence. Thank you, Counsel Par. And the number will be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This videotape will be Prosecution Exhibit 389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me first of all ask the witness to make the solemn declaration. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I should like to draw your attention to the following. On the 7th of September, the Defence received from the Prosecution a document -- rather, a statement of the witness present here. Attached to this statement there were also some addenda, called Annex 1, Annex B; and another document, which is a copy of a combat order. The introductory part of this material shows that the expert witness gives his opinion on the basis of his knowledge and documents and facts shown him. And if we look, Your Honours, at this document provided by the expert witness, we see that in the first part, he addresses the military doctrine principles of command and leadership; that in the second part, the expert witness was given a task of answering a question: How did my defendant embrace those principles of management and leadership? And for this purpose, the witness analysed, as he says, six documents. Then the expert witness was to answer another question, on the basis of yet another four documents: How, and in which assumed likely situation, was my defendant on the day of the 16th of April? It would be all right, except that six documents, Your Honours, considered by the expert, of those six documents, three have not been verified and their authenticity has not been confirmed in this Court. These are documents of the 30th of January, '93, on the casualties. These are documents which the defendant signed. Then the minutes of the 16th of September, '93, on a deployment for help; and 8th of April, '93, an order of the 8th of April, '93. We have no problem with that, or at least not too much of a problem for us. But the other three documents which were also considered by the witness are documents which were adopted by this Court on the 6th of October last year during the testimony of Witness AA. This testimony was given in closed session, so the three documents -- 250, 251, and 252 -- are documents which must remain confidential forever. Let us move on. Of another four documents which the witness also looked into, and which were to serve as a basis for the conclusion on the hypothetical role of Vlado Santic on the 16th of April, these are documents which were admitted on the 14th of July this year by this Court in a closed session. That is a session closed for the public. Moreover, these documents, in another case before this Tribunal, are under seal. Now, my question is: How could the Prosecutor disclose these documents to a witness who is testifying in public, show them to him, and ask him to give his expert opinion on the basis of those documents? Had the Prosecutor not shown this to the witness, then his statement would not go beyond military doctrine. What gives me concern is the documents which were presented at the closed session, with all the consequences deriving from that. When you read these documents, you see that they create major difficulties for the defence of Vladimir Santic, and had the expert witness been deprived of this information, his finding would have been completely different. So this is my first question, and I should like to ask you kindly to answer this question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. I think there is one fundamental quantum difference between the normal witnesses as to fact and an expert witness. It is not uncommon, where expert witnesses are called upon, that they are in receipt of otherwise confidential information. One could imagine an equivalent position of a trial where, for instance, some kind of medical expert is required -- a psychiatrist, psychologist, whatever -- to comment on matters. I have recent experience, as Your Honours have, of matters relating to the human memory and the effect of trauma and stress on a person. Now, in order for the expert to be properly briefed, there may have to be the disclosure of matters that have been raised in closed session, private session, documents that are otherwise private, and documents which are otherwise perhaps not even in evidence, but are of importance to assist the expert in the preparation of their expert testimony. Now, obviously, in the course of examining such an expert, we are mindful, we all have to be mindful, of the fact that the protective measures for witnesses are preserved, and obviously reference is made accordingly to be careful in that respect. But of course, the whole purpose of closed session and other things is the protection of the identity and safety of witnesses. It is not to exclude experts from access to information, nor indeed to exclude the Defence, the Prosecution, or the Chamber from valuable information. Accordingly, as an expert witness is to be briefed in that respect, I respectfully submit that it is appropriate and proper, with due security, to do so, and to that extent an expert witness becomes almost part of the team, the Prosecution or the Defence. That is perhaps equally evidenced by the fact that in domestic courts, and, indeed, as experienced in the Chambers of this Tribunal, often expert witnesses can sit in and listen to the testimony of their colleagues and of other expert witnesses for the other side, which of course is contrary to the normal principles for fact witnesses, for obvious reasons. So I would suggest that in fact my friend's objections regarding these documents are in fact ill-founded, on the basis that they are necessary for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that there is not some point in this. These rules are insisted on by the Prosecution in particular, that there should be no leeway and there should be no way in which people can find out. If you're going to show these documents to somebody else, ought you not first of all to seek the leave of the Trial Chamber before you do so? Otherwise, presumably, it's open to any party to show the documents, if you're right, Mr. Blaxill, to whoever they might think might be an expert, without referring to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I appreciate your point, Your Honour. The answer I would give to that is that I think, firstly, we are of course mindful of being bound by protective measures, and that it is therefore important to try and ensure the confidentiality of such material. And the second thing is that I do recall -- if I recall correctly, and I have no doubt Your Honours will correct me if I'm wrong -- but that sometimes matters are, in a sense, suppressed by the Chamber, but one uses such terminology as "except as necessary in the course of preparation of the Defence," or something of that nature, which I know to me is indicative, Your Honour, that clearly there would be, obviously, occasions envisaged where certain materials have to be communicated in the course of preparation; presumably, if that applies to the Defence, equally the preparation of the Prosecution. I think I cannot really answer you further than that. As regards should it be a practice to apply to the Trial Chamber for it, it's not something that we have yet been aware should be the case; perhaps it is something to address for the future. I would suggest, though, Your Honour, that we do try, obviously, being bound by such confidentiality as has been ordered by a Chamber, we try to observe that within the confines of preparing the case properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite true that the situation could have been prevented by seeking the leave of the Chamber, or perhaps in another way, of course, had the witness been shown these documents for the first time here in a closed session, but that is not true. He already was in possession of all the information that he needs, so that his answers are conditioned by some knowledge, by the knowledge of facts he shouldn't have had, and that will go to the detriment of the accused Vladimir Santic. I think there is room here for the application of Rule 89(B).

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me; I do apologise. Not 89(B), but 89(D). 89(D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Bench believes that the Prosecution should have sought leave from the Chamber, leave to show those confidential documents to the witness, expert witness, so we will consider what action should be taken with respect to this failure by the Prosecution to get the authorisation of the Chamber to go ahead. On the other hand, we feel that in light of Rule 89(B), I think 89(B) should be applied. We think that this document should be used by the witness in the examination-in-chief or cross-examination, and so we will proceed on the basis that he is aware, and he may be put questions with respect to those documents. So we will go ahead; however, we reserve the right to consider what action to take with respect to the conduct of the Prosecution. As I say, we feel that actually Rule 89(B) should be applied, because we feel that we will apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before our Chamber, and which are consonant with the spirit of the statute and the general principles of law. The search for truth is the prevailing principle, and in light of this principle, we think we can proceed along the lines suggested by the Prosecution. This is our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Indeed, obviously, we shall be conscious of any issues of protection in the course of this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, would you please give the Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. My name is Asim Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your date of birth, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of June, 1949, in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What is your present occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm presently with the Federal Ministry of Defence, head of the political affairs department in the sector for defence preparations at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And is that a military post, sir, and does it carry a rank, or do you carry a rank, I should say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: It is a military rank. I am a Brigadier in the army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Have you been a career soldier for the entirety of your working life?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: When I came out of the secondary school, I enrolled in the military academy. As of 1973 to this day, I have been a professional military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And when you commenced your military career, in which armed force did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I enrolled in the military academy in 1969 in Belgrade, and this is an academy for ground troops for the army, in infantry details. I completed it in 1973, and I was given the 1st Officer rank and I have been with the army ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And during the earlier part of your military career, have you had any particular speciality in which you worked, such as infantry, artillery, or any particular branch?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Infantry is my speciality and, therefore, I discharged various duties in the Yugoslav People's Army, from the lowest one -- that is, platoon commander -- to the head of the brigade staff in 1992, when, for reasons known to all, because of the military and political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, I quit the Yugoslav People's Army and joined the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I can turn back to Yugoslav national army. What was the basic strategic role assigned to the Yugoslav national army?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The strategy of the armed forces, and then, within the armed forces, the Yugoslav People's Army, was the defence of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia; that is to say, it was based on defence tactics and strategy.
