Or to put it more aptly, outside the boundaries of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, never were any actions planned outside the borders of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And on what basis was the manpower of the JNA organised? Did you have active and reserve and other kinds of forces?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army, in the armed forces, we have to say, of the former Yugoslavia, there was the Yugoslav People's Army, and it had manoeuvring and active units, as we put it in professional terms. Active units consisted of officers, commissioned and noncommissioned; that is to say, these were professionals. Also, soldiers who were doing their military service. Also, partly there were civilians who were employed in accordance with the regulations that were then in force. That was the active component of the Yugoslav People's Army. In the Yugoslav People's Army there were war units too, and the war units were composed as follows: of reserve soldiers, reserve officers, reserve noncommissioned officers. Perhaps it is important for you to note that if we take into account, for example, any formation of an active unit -- for example, a brigade -- the organisation and formation of such an active unit, a brigade, consisted of less people in terms of manpower and technical weapons, et cetera, as compared to a war unit of the same level. That is to say that the Yugoslav People's Army covered for this when need be and when orders were issued by persons in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what were the general obligations, to your knowledge, of the citizens of the former Yugoslavia in relation to these various manpower principles of the JNA? What duties did the civilians have -- or citizens, I'm sorry, have?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: It is well-known that the former Yugoslavia had a system of All People's Defence. The system of All People's Defence and social self-defence, as it was called, included all the citizens of the former Yugoslavia from the age of 18 up to the age of 60 in the case of men, or the age of 55 in the case of women, as regulated by basic legislation in this field. The system of All People's Defence served the purposes of the defence of the entire territory and engaging all potentialities; that is to say, material and human resources for defence purposes. Now, how were these units recruited, manned, and organised? We can analyse this in several ways and try to explain it. The core of the matter is as follows: In active units, as I already pointed out, there were professional commissioned and noncommissioned officers and soldiers who were currently doing their military service. In the system that prevailed then, all the soldiers who would complete their military service, upon completing their military service, would report to the secretariat for defence in their own municipality, in the territory where they lived, and then they would be transferred to the status of reserve soldier or reserve noncommissioned officer or reserve officer, depending on whether that soldier, while doing his military service, attended a course for noncommissioned officers or a school for reserve officers. This was organised very well, at a very high level, in the former Yugoslav People's Army. So there was a base, so to speak, where people would prepare themselves, while doing their military service, for situations of crisis and even war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What would be the position under that system regarding those who were not deemed fit for active military service or perhaps too old for active military service?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The system of All People's Defence envisaged for such matters as well; that is to say, these specific cases. Therefore, such persons -- this was not a rule, but as a principle these persons were recorded and organised in civilian protection units. This could have been a young man, aged 18, if according to law he was not fit for military service; also, persons over the age of 60. Civilian defence, civilian protection, was a very broad concept, and it included practically all spheres of life and work of an organised people, of an organised community, starting from those situations that have to be resolved in a situation of crisis, like earthquakes, floods, et cetera, all the way to those basic logistics matters; for example, preparing food, giving first-aid, evacuation, et cetera. That is to say that there was a very wide range for engaging persons in civilian protection units. All of this together comprised the system of All People's Defence, and this was a specific concept which was organised in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, very briefly, if you can, Brigadier, will you just give us some idea of the methods used to mobilise people in times of emergency and how quickly that could be done?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In all units -- that is to say, of the Yugoslav People's Army, of the Territorial Defence, and of civilian protection -- there were certain plans for mobilisation. These plans were mobilised when necessary; that is to say, when there would be a critical situation. The competent authority in the municipality, in the Republic, in the unit, that is to say, at all three levels, was in charge of activating this system of mobilisation and calling up the members of these reserve units, the members of civilian protection units, in one of the following ways: The system of the call-up services, which operated very well. There were different ways of call-ups. People could be called up directly, by way of a messenger, also through various communications, or in any other way which yielded certain results; that is to say, in order to achieve the set objective in the best possible way. Most often it was the messenger service that was resorted to. That is to say that there were messengers who, at a given point in time, when orders were issued by the competent authorities, were discharged to local communities, units, et cetera. And according to a specific outline that existed in every unit, they called up the reservists; that is to say the members of the civilian defence in the case of civilian defence units. Every individual knew where his position was. Everybody was aware of his wartime position. Everybody was aware of his place of mobilisation; that is to say, where they were rounded up and what duties they were to perform. If we're talking about soldiers, soldiers also had equipment issued to them. They did not have weapons on them at the time; they only had equipment; whereas the members of the civilian protection units did not have any equipment either. For example, if these were fire brigades or any other special units, then they knew which equipment they were supposed to use and in which way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we go one step further, what was the basic unit structure of the Yugoslav national army? Into what kind of size and nature of units was it divided?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The units of the Yugoslav People's Army were organised into arms and services. It was prescribed by law exactly which arms and which services; that is to say, the infantry, the artillery, engineering units, et cetera. Then also the medical corps, the veterinary corps, weather forecasting service, et cetera. That is to say that the units of the Yugoslav People's Army had their own arms and services. The organisation and formation of the Yugoslav People's Army, until 1988, was as follows: At the level of every republic there were armies, respectively, with their respective seats in the capitals of these republics. For example, in Sarajevo there was the seat of the 7th Army. Its seat was in Sarajevo. The seat of the 5th Army was in Zagreb, et cetera. The armies included lower-level units such as divisions, brigades, battalions, companies, platoons, down to that lowest level. Towards the end of 1998 and the beginning of 1999, a strategic reorganisation was carried out within the Yugoslav People's Army. Then army commands within republics were abolished and four military districts were established. They included a somewhat broader territory and involved a wider range of responsibility than the commands of the armies. There was the Belgrade, Zagreb, Skopje, and Split military districts, respectively. That is to say that these military districts transcended republican boundaries, and in this way republican centres -- some of them, rather -- lost the status they enjoyed previously; that is to say, to have this high command. A lower organisational level was that of corps, and within a corps there were brigades, and then further on, as in any army, battalions, companies, platoons, and lower-level units. That was the general organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when we get to 1992 and we have the split of the republics within the former Yugoslavia, what would you offer by way of comment upon the formation of their military organisations and any relationship to former JNA principles and doctrine?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not quite understand you. Their principles; whose principles?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, let us say that we are aware of different entities coming into being gradually: the army of BiH; the VRS, being the Bosnian Serb; the HVO, the Croatian -- Bosnian Croatian. What relationship or features do you recall vis-a-vis the JNA principles and training?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Basically, the tactics, strategy, and operations are not laws. They're not axioms that are ever changed anywhere in the world in any army. These principles are more or less similar or identical. In the beginning of 1992, it was inevitable, for various reasons that I don't want to go into now, that republican armies were set up, starting from Slovenia via Bosnia-Herzegovina and further on. Basically, in essence, in principle, there was no choice for any newly established army but to take over the established principles of the former Yugoslav People's Army; that is to say, in principle, the tenets of organisation and mode of operation were taken over. However, the distinctions were as follows: These differences were primarily expressed in the potentials of armaments, weapons, and military technical facilities. At that moment, the former Yugoslav People's Army took over, in various ways, the larger part of the available weapons, armaments, and military technical facilities. The Republic of Croatia was in a somewhat more favourable possession. In its garrisons, something remained. That was the agreement that was made: some military equipment and weapons that remained. However, the most unfavourable situation was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the case of the Croat and Bosniak peoples. They had the least amount of these armaments, weapons, and technical facilities, and that is where the greatest difference was. There were also differences that cropped up later in terms of a language approach, so to speak. So, for example, one term that would be used by the Bosniaks would not be applied by the Croats, or the same term would have a different meaning with the Serbs. So these language problems had come to the fore depending on the specific characteristics of the people that was establishing that army. I think you are aware of the fact that the armies and defence systems that were set up at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established, the HVO was established, the army of Republika Srpska was established. There was a specific characteristic involved. The army of Republika Srpska and the HVO, in their system of defence and organisation, relied upon the neighbouring states of Croatia and Yugoslavia, respectively, which was only logical and realistic, and they had a certain degree of cooperation where there were adequate conditions in terms of military assistance, logistics, training, education, et cetera. Those were the elements that differed. However, the basic principles and tenets of organisation were almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Brigadier, can you tell me, please, therefore, what is the common chain of command for the passage of an order that emanates from the top and passes down, say, for a combat operation, through the layers of command?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: All the armies of the world, including these armies of ours that were established, accepted the principles of command as a specific system of managing specific units such as military units. That meant that the army, as a specific organisation, has a system of management and command that differs from that that exists in civilian bodies. That meant that the principles of a single command and of subordination had to be observed. From the top -- that is to say, from the top command downwards, as far as orders are concerned, and from the lowest command to the top command when reporting is concerned -- that is to say that these two principles had to be honoured if military organisation were to be abided by, and they were, in principle, accepted by all armies. Or rather, this chain. Let me be clearer on this. This chain would have to be as follows: The commander of a corps could not issue an order to a commander of a battalion, but he had to issue orders to the commander of a brigade, and then he had to issue orders to the commander of the battalion, et cetera, et cetera. So everybody had to take care of a particular level. And it also works the other way around. As far as reporting is concerned, it had to go from a lower-level unit towards a higher-level unit. And in that respect it could not have happened that reporting would go two or three steps higher up in the chain of command. I already pointed out that strategy and tactics are not mathematics and physics. There are some special cases when it could have happened that a report would be sent in a different way. However, in that case, if I was in a position to send a report to my superior officer that was two or three steps above me, I was duty-bound to inform my immediate superior officer as well. At any rate, the principle of subordination had to be respected and was respected. Of course, I shall say what was truly realistic in our practice. In the initial stage of the war in particular -- I think that this was also characteristic of the army of Republika Srpska, of the BH army, and of the HVO -- there were some doubts in the beginning. People were unsure, especially those who were not professional soldiers, who until then were not professionally engaged in such matters and who were not professional soldiers or professional officers. However, that was soon overcome, so that part fell into place too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, you say that an order would be transmitted down through very defined levels of command, but at what point in the chain does the company commander fit in, in terms of the flow of the order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you're going to understand, but any company commander -- any company commander; it doesn't matter which company we're talking about -- always had to receive orders from his immediate superior officer, and that is the commander of the battalion. Sometime it was called the commander of the division, if it was an artillery unit or a rocket unit, but at any rate it was that level. So that is to say a company commander could receive orders from that level, and that is logical and that is normal, from the commander of the battalion. Always, and in all situations, that is the way it is in principle, and according to the tenets that were applied and according to which we worked in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And about what size of unit was commanded by a company commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: In order to facilitate your understanding, the units that were at company level had varying numbers of persons involved. These were units that had from 100 to 350 people, or -- I don't know; in some cases, perhaps even more. However, these were primarily units numbering 100 to 150 persons. That is to say, this went for the artillery and the infantry. But in specific units, such as rocket units, such as some air force units, special units, these units numbered fewer people. However, the fact that they had less manpower was made up for by the sophisticated equipment they had. For example, a parachute company would be much smaller than an infantry company; then a rocket company would be smaller than an infantry company; then also a signals company. So that is to say that their composition differed, but most often they had 100 soldiers, or even up to 300, depending on the arms or services they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And within the company, what would be the general structure of other smaller units that comprised the company? What would they consist of?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Within companies there were platoons, and there could also be two or three independent squads. For example, if we are talking about an infantry company, it would have a signals squad. It could have a small independent squad for a very specific duty, and usually there were three or four platoons or two or three squads included. That is to say that such a squad would have about 10 people, and platoons would have 20, 25, 30 to 40 people; within that range. There was no rule. All of this was prescribed by way of formations, so it was known quite precisely, according to this formation, how many people a specific platoon should have -- infantry, artillery, rockets, signals, et cetera. So all the elements were prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell me if there was any significance or significant difference that attached to military police units?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: There is no significant difference in terms of organisation and formation, but there was a significant difference, of course, in terms of armament, equipment, and training. Special units, which include, of course, the military police, in practice, always had better equipment, more up-to-date weaponry, and also they had chosen soldiers, because the members of these special units, after all, according to certain characteristics and according to certain principles, did differ from rank-and-file soldiers. So not anybody, so to speak, could have been in these special units. They had to meet certain criteria, such as a level of training and schooling, physical fitness, swiftness, and intellectual capacities. And all special units, including the military police, had special training for the purposes they were intended for. The fact that other units did not have this was only normal, taking into account the entire organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would the presence of something like an antiterrorist platoon be something that would cause you any surprise, or would cause you no surprise, when looking at a military police unit or company?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: There did not exist a strict rule whether it could exist. And it would be only natural, and I believe professional soldiers, if there are some of them here, will know that any unit for a specific task may be attached to a large number of other units, and it is only natural that within a special unit, such as the military police, there is also one such unit. As for the tasks of the military police as prescribed by the former Yugoslav People's Army, and in the new army set up, this was at the level of a doctrine. They also had antiterrorist platoons and their criminal department, their traffic units, and that is all the units charged with special tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, just to confirm your contact with or knowledge of the HVO, did you at any time have any dealings with or in parallel to the HVO in, say, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I did have an opportunity, but especially in the early days of the war. In April '92, my first duty was to organise the Territorial Defence in the area of Konjic. That was the first time that I came across men and units of the HVO, and we co-operated very successfully, both in Konjic -- and in Konjic at that time, we set up the joint TO command. Rather, the commander specifically was a Bosniak, and the head of the staff was a Croat. The first missions in that area at that time, April and May, they carried out jointly. And I believe that at that time, in that area, specifically, where I was there at the time, our co-operation was quite commendable. When I returned from Konjic, I came to Visoko, and from there to various other towns in Central Bosnia, where I was engaged in the organisation and betterment of the territorial organisation. Those towns included Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Kakanj. And, say, in Travnik, I already came across a problem. In a restaurant called Plave Vode, I had a meeting with Mr. Kordic, and there, based on the -- he refused to set up the joint command modelled on what we had done in Konjic. But then, at that time, we neither had any problem of talking openly; they simply did not accept this concept, the joint command. So we proceeded to do as we had planned to by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But as a result, Brigadier, were you able to observe the kind of command structure adopted by the HVO as much as the command structure adopted by the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was basically involved in planning, in the operative administration, I knew about that both from reports, from conversations and meetings with our colleagues in the HVO, which we held both in '92 and even during the conflict, during the negotiations, and after that. So I do know that, and I do not think there was anything peculiar particularly to it. I have this information, I am quite familiar with it, and I do not think there is any particularly special specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may now, Brigadier, return to the role of a company commander. What are the basic duties of a company commander in terms of running the company, administratively, or in disciplinary terms?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The duties, that is -- and I have now to link it with the former Yugoslav People's Army. At any level, whether it be a platoon, a company, a battery, or whatever, there were certain rules applicable to it, and those were combat rules. There were corps combat rules, division combat rules, brigade combat rules, company combat rules, squad combat rules, down to the squad. Each of these sets of rules defined -- stipulated clearly the rights and duties of the commander of the given unit, and this was very specific and very precisely set. Those principles were accepted because no military organisation can function without that. It would be an illusion, and I do not think that there have been -- the changes in the chain of command have changed over time only with regard to the means and resources, but basically it has always been the same since time immemorial, so that there were the duties of the platoon commander or company commander. Now, which were the duties of a company commander? He had his duties prescribed for peacetime, and he also had his duties spelled out for wartime, so there was a distinction between those two sets of duties. As for the peacetime duties, it was the organisation of life and work, organisation of training, improving military preparedness and everything that has to do with the life and work of a unit. His special duties were spelled out for critical situations, for cases of crisis and wartime. The most important duty in wartime was that every commander, including the company commander, needs to maintain the necessary level of combat preparedness, or rather preparedness for the execution of whatever tasks which lies ahead; it doesn't matter which task. His basic, his chief duty was to sustain such a level of combat preparedness which would ensure that the task which he will be issued, he can carry out successfully. Now, if you want me to tell you what a company commander does after he has been issued his task, I will do that, if you want me -- I do not know whether you want me to go into all this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, I would like you to say that when, let us say, a form of combat operation is ordered, what kind of order does the company commander receive, and what actions does he take in respect of that order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The process in this annex which you mentioned in the beginning, I explained it because I wanted you to understand it quite clearly, and there I listed all the details. They are as follows: After he has been given a task -- and I am referring to a commander at the level of the company, a company commander, shall I say, and that officer, so he can receive those orders from the battalion commander directly if the situation warrants it. If it is permitted by the place, by the time, and the combat situation, then the battalion commander can summon him and give him that task, or it can be served on him by a courier or a messenger or an authorised person. As an exception, his task can be issued him by communicating equipment, or by cable, but that is avoided. Yet tasks are issued when combat is under way, and then cable telegrams may be used. But that is in use very seldom. Now, after receiving his orders, a company commander then, having learned what his mission is from the battalion commander -- or in whatever way; it doesn't really matter -- then he studies this mission. So it is followed by, shall I say, intellectual process, and the commander studies, therefore, this task and the order to see what it is that the battalion commander wants of him. Having finished that, he makes an assessment of the situation and then notifies his subordinates about the task. His subordinates are platoon commanders and perhaps some squad commanders. Now, how does the company commander go about informing his subordinates? There is a subordinate, an inferior technical unit to a company, so it would be best if the platoon commanders were issued their orders on the ground, in the field. Why? Because they are small units, and in practice, usually in a particular area, in a particular zone, specific tasks are then given them, because the platoons are the end executors of a given task. So it would be logical for the company commander to summon his platoon commanders, to take them to a point, to an observation point, which is most suited to his explaining the task to his subordinates and to then issue them individual orders, if the situation permits that. If the situation permits that, then he may issue the orders to a platoon commander at one point, to another one at a different point, and to a third one again at a third point. So if the situation permits it, then he moves from the position of one platoon to the position of the other platoon, and we call it the command or reconnaissance on the ground, and there he issues specific orders to his men, to his subordinates. Now, in the course of this process, when he issues his orders, it is very important to define questions as to the -- what is the purpose, what is the objective of an activity or a campaign or the mission that is to follow; which is the specific task; how the coordinated action should be organised with the units which are either on the right or the left flank or ahead or in the rear; how to organise communication along two lines, both vertically up the chain of command -- that is, to the superiors -- and how to organise communication horizontally, with units of the same rank. So they define the logistics and the manner in which the logistics will be ensured, and to all intents and purposes all those questions which need to be resolved so as to carry out the mission with as few casualties as possible and with as much success as possible. That would be, briefly, the description of how the company commanders behave after they were issued orders. After a company commander has done this, regular platoon commanders now have the orders, and after that, after he had prepared this and issued his orders, he also needs from time to time to control how his orders are carried out; he is bound, that is, to supervise how his orders are carried out. And that can be done in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL

I would, at the latest, I think, be finishing within the first 20 to 30 minutes tomorrow, if not finishing the examination this morning.

utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands, yes.

utterances.text: Thank you.

That is, we do not object to that, but we should only like to have an additional meeting with her as regards a part of her statement that she made to the Prosecutor. We are not asking for plenty of time; we are only asking for half an hour, and of course, only if the witness agrees to that. So we should like the Court to notify the witness about this, and only if she is willing to do so, and we are quite ready to conduct this conversation with her in the presence of various people from this Court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we deny the motion, the oral motion made by Counsel Radovic and supported by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, in the light of the reasons set out by the Prosecutor. Of course, Defence counsel will be able, it goes without saying, to cross-examine the witness tomorrow when she comes. So we can now move on, and Mr. Blaxill, you may resume your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Brigadier, if we may move on, sir: Once the company commander has received his orders and has issued his instructions to his platoon commanders and subordinates, what is the role of the company commander when his men go into action, into active combat?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: The duty of all commanders in combat, after the combat has started, then they must constantly monitor the combat operations from the command post or a detached command post, and for larger units there can be a certain compound with facilities, with shelters and the like, or four smaller units. Those may be some observation points equipped, or perhaps vehicles, so they may command on the move. There may be a command combat vehicle. So there are different ways in which a commander, once the combat operations have started, will monitor these combat operations. And specifically when it comes to the company commander, the company commander needs to do -- needs to monitor it from the combat deployment of his company; that is, somewhere within the middle, between the first and the second line, in an attack some 3 to 500 metres from the squads in the first line. That is the principle. So a company commander, though, follows the evolution of combat operations, receives reports, and on the basis of these reports and on the basis of his own --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My learned friend has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but I had to interrupt this. But now I should like to take you back to what I said before, that the opinion -- or rather, that the documents which the witness had before him are affecting his thoughts. If you're following carefully what the witness is saying, he is talking about combat operations, and the offensive ones to begin with, because he's assuming that the documents shown him were orders for attack, and now he's hypothesising individual situations as being that the command -- the company commander is there, and there when -- during an attack. But if he had not those documents before him, then he wouldn't be hypothesising those platoon offensive situations and placing a platoon or company commanders in this or that situation. If you really could see these documents which the witness saw, I assure you that these documents were the basis. He constantly talks about offensive combat operations, and yet combat operations may also be defensive. But he assumed that the documents, which he analysed from the point of view of the defence, and that they include offensive activities. So that was my warning, and I can recognise that in what the witness is saying now. I really apologise for interrupting, but I assure you that my assumption is quite correct, because this witness does not refer at all to defence operations. He constantly speaks about offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may reply. If that is the way it is reading, obviously that's one thing, but as I recall my questions so far, I mentioned the word "combat operations." To my mind, that doesn't fall on either side of the coin. It is defensive, offensive, whatever. It simply is combat operations. I had hoped I'd refined my questioning to general principles, but at the same time, I'm trying to get at quickly to the nub of the issue so that I don't take enormous amounts of Your Honours' time on generalisations. I think these -- I think it is irrelevant and inappropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I agree. So you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to clarify something. The principal forms of combat operations are the offensive and the defence. So these are two basic types of the combat, but I can talk about combat when encircled, I can talk about ambush, I can talk about anything, but that is a form of combat operation, and all the activities that I mentioned, whether they be reconnaissance, ambush, attack, defence? All superiors called "commanders" are the same; that is, they must monitor the situation. It does not really matter where they are. That is true, absolutely true. They must monitor the situation. They must receive reports. They must effect the operation, and it doesn't matter what it is: reconnaissance, attack, defence, whatever. So basically, it is all the same. It does not really matter whether it is defence, or attack, ambush, breakthrough from encirclement or whatever, reconnaissance or whatever -- there is quite a range of these operations -- but commanders' duties are always the same, except -- except, and that is the only difference -- his position, his actual location may vary depending on whether it's an attack or defence or ambush or reconnaissance, so on and so forth, and that can be the only difference. And all other of his duties are absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, you've mentioned, I believe, that the company commander would have to -- would probably be in the field or near the field of operations by his troops, whether this be defensive or offensive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And again applying general principles, what would a company commander be expected to do whilst his people were performing the operation, as the thing is ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: So once again, irrespective of the combat operation, respective of the name it carries, a company commander follows the situation from his observation point or from his command post, either in situ or on the move. He receives the reports from his subordinates and, on the basis of those, assesses the situation, issues additional orders to his subordinates, depending on the evolution of the situation on the ground, and within this -- with the time set by the orders, sets -- with set intervals, sends reports to his superior; that is, the battalion commander. If necessary, he may do that at regular intervals, or perhaps more often, if the situation would warrant something like that. So it's up to him to carefully observe how things are going, to amend his former orders and decisions, fill them in with the new information, and report to their superiors. Those are the duties of any commander. It does not really matter what the rank of the unit is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would you expect a company commander to leave the area of operations at any time or would a company commander ever leave the area of operations?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: A company commander -- a company commander is not a good company commander, or any commander who leaves the area where combat operations are conducted is not a good commander, and he, therefore, is subjected to sanctions unless the reason is justified. But I cannot go into that. Some of his reasons for leaving the area may be of a private, of a grave -- of a very grave nature; for instance, if in his family some family situation -- grave family situation has evolved. In that case, he must seek permission from his superior to leave. It can happen in practice and even in times of war and even in the worst situations. But fact of the matter is, if he has left -- if he leaves on his own, then he has to account for that. But now you always seek leave from the Chamber and that is the correct procedure. So he is bound to seek leave from his superior. If he's given that leave, then his superior will say, "Yes. You are free to go, and Mr. So-and-so, called so-and-so, occupying the rank of, will then -- will be substituting, will be taking your place."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, moving on from that general role of the company commander, what do you recall to be the duties of the military police when it came to a time of war as opposed to their duties in a time of peace?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: Also in this supplementary paper that I provided, I referred to the rules of the military police of the former JNA and the rules for the military police in the BH army, and I mentioned what the peacetime duties were, what the duties were in cases of imminent danger of war, and what the wartime duties are, and all of that has been spelled out very precisely. The military police carries out military police work in peacetime, in a word, and they vary: providing safety and security for movement, providing for order and discipline, taking action related to ascertaining responsibility of soldiers and officers, and also training for military police purposes as prescribed by the regulations concerned. Military police units belong to the military police itself, to anti-sabotage units, police units, and then traffic units, and sometimes there were some other specialities. Also, there was the crime prevention service, and also sometimes perhaps some reconnaissance units with special tasks. Also, divers. It depends on where the actual unit is and what the higher unit above that military police unit is. During the war -- I'm talking about the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO, and the army of Republika Srpska -- the military police was used wherever necessary. In most cases it was used for combat operations, regardless of which army we're talking about, because there were no other forces that were available for carrying out these tasks, although in peacetime they did also provide for the security of the command headquarters, of movement, and they manned checkpoints. That's what the military police did as well. In the initial stages of the war a bit more, but then they became even more capable of carrying out their tasks. As I said at the beginning, this was in the BH army as well. Later on, these units got the most responsible tasks to carry out, because they had the equipment and the trained people to do that kind of thing. Now, if you want me to list all these duties, I can. I can read it out from the paper I prepared, but I don't think it's necessary for me to list each and every one of them. Perhaps it is important to mention here that in practice, there was perhaps a deviation in the case of the military police. Indeed, military police units were used literally for each and every task, although that was not envisaged in the basic principles that the military police be engaged in each and every task, but in practice that's the way it was in every one of these three armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you just indicate to me, please, what tasks those would have been in a combat context, be it a defensive situation or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a practical example. This was a concrete bit of experience we had. The units of the military police, in this war of ours that went on in Bosnia from 1992 onwards, all three armies -- I'm not only talking about the military police. These commanders know very well there were other units that were called special units and military police units. They differed. But they were not very fond of carrying out defence assignments. They kept saying, "We are not linesmen," as they call themselves. "We don't really like doing that kind of thing." That's how it was in practice. However, "We would like to carry out offensive tasks. That's what we are good at. Don't make us hold defence lines. We are special units, and we haven't got the time or conditions to dwell on such matters of lesser importance." That's the way it was in the BH army, in the army of Republika Srpska, and in the HVO. We can see from the reports that can be seen now, most citations during the war were received by these units. This can be seen in practice from reports, and this was also publicised in the media. Also, when the anniversaries of these units were commemorated, it was usually the military police and reconnaissance units that were highly commended, that received citations. That's what it was like in practice, although they did carry out defence tasks too when it was absolutely necessary and when there was no other way out, but this was very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your preparation for --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC
